While in the assembly at Miman, I dreamed one night and wrote a couplet upon the wall: "Snow dots the balustrades; the temple lies beneath emerald lapis lazuli. Clouds span the heavens;
people return within the midst of crimson lotuses. A full year has passed, yet I continue to turn the wheel of worldly affairs.
Alas, I do not know whether the Reward Land (vipāka-kṣetra) will truly manifest anywhere at all. Tsk! One must strictly avoid speaking of dreams.
Master Puci was a native of Yuzhang. His appearance was extraordinary. Initially, he visited Xuedang Xing at Wugu in Quzhou;

subsequently, he traveled to Huxiang and met Miaoxi before Huayan Peak. He endured many hardships amidst miasmic vapors and formed a close friendship with Wang Shengxi, the provincial examination head (Zhuangyuan).
Wang was a native of Shangrao who recommended Puci to reside at Huaiyu Monastery; this master was the successor to Nan Chan Master.
When Wang later governed Min, he summoned [Zhao] using an elephant bone. During the Qiandao era, he was commissioned by imperial decree to preside over Shuangjing Monastery;

he was repeatedly summoned to the inner court, where he greatly delighted the Emperor’s countenance. He was specially granted the title Chan Master Huiri. In his later years, he again received an edict to return to Xuefeng.
Old Master Sheng of Gushan composed a preface stating: "The celestial sphere remains unmoving, yet in an instant it turns the heavens."
Above, the winds and clouds gather; the Great Function manifests before us. Transversely and longitudinally, they hang within the realm like sun and moon.
We rejoice in this once-in-a-century encounter, hoping for the auspiciousness of a reunion every millennium. His virtue is ever-renewing, and people seek out those of long-standing excellence.

Such a person as you has established his Way in the southern Min and the two Zhe regions, where your affinity accords with Xueqiao and Wufeng. Elder brother before and younger brother behind, you have naturally earned a fine reputation. In the past...

Having departed from here, they have now returned and all respectfully received the imperial edicts. The Buddha-dharma has been revitalized; throughout the nine provinces and the four seas, all perceive the will of Heaven.

You alone have received the sovereign’s personal knowledge, while eminent dukes and great ministers all revere and praise you as their teacher. Just as you were about to soar like a phoenix upon the vermilion steps of the palace, you were suddenly startled by the return of the pearl from Hepu.
Behold the white horse coming from the East—what need is there to wait for a green robe to sweep the ground? Over one thousand dragons...
O elephant-like monk, as you stand gazing upon the elephant’s carriage and turning back, this ancestral site of the Patriarchs for three hundred years shall once again witness the wooden ball roll.
We pray that you will uphold the secret seal and respond to our sincere devotion. It is heard that your meritorious conditions are most excellent, rarely equaled in recent times;
yet, regarding the ultimate point, the monastic communities do not fully place their trust in you, which results in your person being suppressed and your reputation perishing.
○ Chan Master Tien-an Yida was a native of Jianchang. He practiced alongside the dharma-brother Fotiao Dandao.
Initially, he visited Yue’an Guo, and subsequently visited Ying’an Hua. While Hua was residing at Guizong, Tien-an served as his attendant;

Hua took a great liking to him. Tien-an was solitary and aloof, refusing to engage with the world. Hua once inscribed a verse upon his portrait, saying: "Hanging the whisk, holding the whisk—his entire capacity is fully manifest."
Appearing and disappearing; one shout deafens the ears for three days. But tell me, was it Mazu who was at fault, or was it Baizhang?

Attendant Zongyi simply brought this up in such a manner. During the Qiandao era, he appeared in the world and resided at Qingshan in Tai, later moving to Xiangfu in Qu, ultimately succeeding Yue’an—truly not forgetting what he had received. There is a eulogy for his portrait that says: "Turning the [scriptures] over..."
Regarding the four elements and five aggregates, he thoroughly realized the single aperture that transcends them. With heart and soul laid bare for others, he was instead met with secret derision.
"The pupil in the eye blows an iron whistle; holding a shell to measure the ocean is but a waste of spirit.
An iron pot brewing tea is not the same as a small cauldron. Later, he moved from Jiahe to Shushan and Yangshan, residing twice at Xuefeng before his passing.
○ Xuetang (Snow Hall) once gave a formal discourse to the practitioner Yuanyou, saying:

"When the Elder of Yunju Ga'an was serving as the Head Seat at Longmen, whenever he addressed the assembly, he would invariably say: 'One must know that there are those who possess true understanding.

Later, while attending his instructions, I once requested to hear his explanation of this. His words were: 'In a vast multitude, those who are base are always many, whereas those who possess true understanding..."

The common are always few; those who are vulgar are easy to associate with, while the wise are difficult to befriend. To strive for one's aspirations amidst such conditions is like a single person fighting ten thousand men.
When the force of vulgar habits is exhausted, one becomes a truly outstanding man of immeasurable capacity.

From this point on, I have recited these words throughout my life: if the breath (vital energy) overcomes the will, one becomes a petty person; if the will overcomes the breath, one becomes an upright and virtuous gentleman.

It is only when will and spirit are in harmony that one becomes a sage who has attained the Way. When there are those who are stubborn and headstrong, refusing to accept admonition or instruction, it is their spirit that causes them to be so.
When Jīvaka was about to die, the hundred medicinal herbs all wept, saying: "While Jīvaka is in the world, we have a use;
after Jīvaka dies, there will be no one in the world who recognizes us. This is a metaphor for all phenomena in the world. Not yet—
When I left the household life, I was at the age of twenty. The Layman Du once said to me: "If there is no master within, one is not upright;
if there is no master without, one does not act. From that time on, I have followed these words throughout my life.

Whether establishing myself as a layman or leaving home to study the Way, and even until the end of my years in presiding over the assembly, I have relied upon this as a scale or a steelyard determines lightness and weight, or as a compass and square determine right angles.
...to achieve squareness and roundness. To depart from this is to lose the standard in every matter.
Yuan You, you must exert yourself in this! Master Yingbin Su Ziyou was once exiled to Jinyang. There, he shared a spiritual affinity with Zhenjing.
He once sent a verse to Master Shun of Xiangcheng, which said: "Melting away infinite matters, they all become a single piece of mind. This mind..."
It does not exist. From antiquity until the present. It is also said: "As if seen, yet as if lost; how many times have we met and laughed? Herein there is no beginning or end;
there is no need to measure it in inches. If you wish to know Old东坡 (Sōngp'o), he was a truly eminent man.
Lately he has come to know this matter, and thus he no longer reads books. Sōngp'o was also in a place of exile when he heard that you were deeply inclined toward this.
He named his residence "Dongxuan" (Eastern Porch) and wrote a poem in jest, containing the line: "Please bring Elder Dongxuan here. Ziyou replied:
"Even if Sheng comes, he will have no use; Xuetang already has its own Senior Brother.
He also once composed a poem in the style of Yuanming, which says: "The Buddha-dharma prevails in the Central Plains; Confucian scholars are ashamed to discuss it. Its merit..."
I offer this almsgiving into the profound darkness; what have I done to betray my contemporaries? This region has long been steeped in impurity, a murky mass where the monastic robes are nameless.

They attend to their livelihoods and guard their households, sitting idly and causing these people to harbor doubts. They do not yet know that wine and meat are not the path, nor do they bid farewell to birth and death.

Yet, in our province of Min, the Buddhist services burn brightly and are inconceivable. Many children born here are exceptionally gifted; the karmic retribution I receive shall not deceive you. At this time—
There is the Eye of the True Dharma; let it shine forth once more. Who would say that the local elite do not exist? Please recite this poem of mine for them.

Chao Guanglu Huijing thoroughly mastered the scriptures of both the inner and outer teachings. In his later years, he composed the *Fazang Suijin* (Golden Nuggets from the Dharma-Treasury), which circulated among both Confucians and Buddhists.
His words were deeply earnest in promoting moral transformation. A Confucian said: "A scholar who possesses ambition must not lack learning."

Therefore, a Buddhist scripture states: "For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no difference in principle. If one understands these words yet merely follows them while neglecting practice, it is truly to be lamented.

I have observed the texts of the Three Teachings and roughly perceived their intent that one must study: the *Book of Changes* says of the Confucian gentleman, "He advances his virtue and cultivates his deeds";
Laozi of the Daoist tradition says, "When the superior man hears the Way, he applies himself diligently to its practice"; and [the Buddha] said of the Śrāvakas...
The *Jijing* (Sutra on Accumulated Sayings) states: "Just as a great dragon has accomplished what was to be done, laid down its heavy burden, and nearly attained its own benefit.
I have participated in his studies and investigations; although I know that the phrasing of this passage is unconventional, there is no doubt that his virtue stems from his learning.
Furthermore, his resolve in old age was profound, and his influence extended to the very end. His final teaching, even after ten thousand kalpas—
It cannot be altered.

○ Chan Master Dayuanyizhi was a native of Siming. He succeeded Daolin Yi; Yi had studied under Yushan Ju, who had studied under Huanglong Nan. Thus, he personally received the essential tenets of Huanglong.
His "Verses on the Three Barriers" (*Sanguan song*) and his "Critical Comments on Ancient Cases" (*Nianggu*) were widely circulated.
At the beginning of his tenure at Conglin, Miaoxi heard that [Zhaozhou] was straightforward and did not engage in formal affairs, so he was not particularly pleased with him.

However, upon examining his *Niangu* (Commentaries on Ancient Cases), he struck the desk in appreciation and praised him, saying, "This is truly the authentic transmission of Huanglong. He then took up his brush and inscribed these four lines after it:
"The life-vein of the Seven Buddhas, the eyes of the patriarchs; simply look into this record, and all is spontaneously present. Thus it began.
Only those who study this will come to know that the applications of these two masters were originally no different from one another.
Yet Zhi once said to others: "The activities of Dahui Zonggao and Miaoxi did not fall short of those of Yantou and Sishin; they can truly be called teachers for a hundred generations.

However, they have merely not yet deliberated upon that matter with this old monk. Had they encountered me even once, I would certainly have caused them to outshine the past and surpass all that came after. Nevertheless—
The two masters never met one another. Zhi passed away at Shishuang; ten days prior to his death, he received the memorial offerings for his disciples.
He ascended the Dharma seat and, sitting upright, passed into extinction. Only then did people realize that Miaoxi was not one who would lightly grant his approval to others.
Miaodao Daoren was the daughter of the Huang family of Yanping. She had visited many venerable masters before eventually seeking out Miaoxi at Mount Jing.
There, Miaoxi asked a monk in his quarters, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is it?
The monk was at a loss for an answer. Daoren, standing outside the gate, heard this and attained a sudden, clear realization. She then informed Miaoxi, who said, "The mulberry..."

An arrow struck a tree; the *zhù* tree exuded sap, which was used to seal the spot where it had been pierced. Later, he opened the hall at Hongfu and addressed the assembly, saying: "Chan is not a matter of conceptual thought;

to set up an intention deviates from the source. The Way transcends all achievement; to build up merit is to lose one's true portion. Beyond sound and outside of phrases, do not seek within the realm of the intellect.
Holding the mechanism of illumination and function, grasping the tongs and hammer of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, wherever there is a Buddha, they act as one another’s counterparts."
Host and guest: where there is no Buddha, the wind whistles through; the mind is tranquil and the spirit at ease; responses are harmonious and sounds are in accord.
For one such as this, tell me, where would you place him? After a long silence, he said: "Crouching under a straw raincoat, standing askew beyond a thousand peaks;
leading water to irrigate vegetables before the Five Elders. He added: "To miss the eyebrows by lowering them is much like wetting one's bed while wide awake."
The public case is now resolved; this is precisely where the clever child falls into the trap. Neither "it is so" nor "it is not so" will do.
A tortoise dragging its tail—neither mind, nor Buddha, nor thing. Nailing a stake into empty space.

Even if you can leave behind all these idle gates and broken doors, you are still hiding a dragon in stagnant water. How shall one express the single phrase that overturns the torrents and topples the mountains?
"Birth-path! When the Great Spirit raised his hand, there was not much to it; yet he split apart the ten thousand myriad peaks of Mount Hua.
Later, when Shuian saw a monk cite this, he placed his hands over his forehead and said, "This matter may indeed be called neither male nor female.
How many men of substance have spent ten or five years within the assembly searching for their heads and failed to find them? Though she was but a woman, she was truly—"
There is the work of a true man; how much it surpasses the fabrications of those "elderly" monks! ○ Master Jiantang:
when he first resided at Guanshan in Rao, for seventeen years he lived by fire-starting and knife-plowing, undergoing every kind of hardship.
Those who dwelt with him were all from the four quarters who had come there of their own accord; thus they could share in the same silence and solitude, unconcerned with worldly matters.
Although his outward appearance was that of a man of humble means and simple integrity, the world came to call him "The Master of the Way of Skillful Means" (Jīdào).
Later, he resided at Yuantong in Jiǔjiāng and widely propagated the teachings of Cí'ān. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The one at Yuantong does not open a pharmacy for the living;
he sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. I wonder which of you, free from calculation and thought, can eat it and have cold sweat pour down your entire body?"

From then on, he moved to the seclusion and tranquility of Taiping. Although the assembly was large, the food in the hall and kitchen was simple and plain; yet none of his brothers dared to speak of it.

Whenever he requested someone to take an office, he invariably followed the method of the late Huanglong: after the morning gruel, he would hang his bowl and face the hall, instructing the attendant to strike the gavel and announce, "I request that such-and-such a person assume this duty. There were none among his brothers who did not comply with him. However, if there were...

If anyone disobeyed, he would immediately rebuke them, saying, "Jiandang does not do things here; where else would you go to do them? Alas! The former masters placed such weight on their words that they employed people with such ease.
How could it be compared to the present day, when one must perform seven kneelings and eight prostrations? My humble feelings are beyond measure.
He was even leaping up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven! Alas for the Buddha! ○ Zheng Xilin, styled Laona (The Old Monk), was a native of Changsha.
He was the dharma heir of Yue’an. While Yue’an resided at Daolin Monastery, Zheng served as the head of the quarters (liàoyuán).
The brothers had already hung their name-boards and entered the room [for formal training]. As a person, he was profoundly sincere and earnest; though he lived...
In a dark room, as if facing a great guest, when brothers see him, their countenances must be solemn. Later, while dwelling at Xilin, his conduct was exemplary;
he had verses and dialogues that followed the *gong'an* (public cases), such as: "Standing on a spark of stone-light, how many difficulties cannot be transcended?
If you possess the Vajra-eye upon the crown of your head, would you ever allow others to hold the fishing rod? This was because he had personally attained the moon.
Anan spoke thus; he was indeed remarkably free from conventional molds. At the beginning, Anan also met Yue’an, whose realization was even more distinct.
He once composed a verse, saying: "At the end of the year, with my lute in arms, where shall I go? To the west of the thirty-six peaks of Luoyang."
In my entire life, I have never set eyes upon you, Master, nor have I been able to hear you chant the "Crows Crying at Night.

One might say that you have truly learned from Liu Xiaohui, yet ultimately did not take his outward traces as your teacher. Those who possess the *śakrāloka* eye upon the crown of their heads will discern this clearly.
Xun Ma was a man of clear insight into the nature of the earth. He once attended upon Fojian, who remarked that because Xun’s physical appearance was so dark and coarse, his merit must be meager.
One day, Fojian happened to say to him, "What a pity—a single bright pearl!"
The beggar who had been given it picked it up. Xun asked him, "Venerable Sir, please keep this safely.
On another day, [Zhaozhou] said, "How have all sentient beings ever attained awakening? Xun replied, "How have all sentient beings ever been deluded?
Suddenly, an attendant passed by in front of them, and Zhaozhou asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The attendant was at a loss for a reply.
Jian said, "When did you ever awaken? Xun immediately called out to an attendant, "Has the evening session ended yet?
The attendant replied, "The session has ended. Xun said, "When did you ever become deluded? Jian shouted at him, "You karmic seed! Get out! Xun said, "Venerable Sir, please keep your voice down;
I fear outsiders might hear us, father and son, here discussing 'sending off' and 'awakening. Jian was greatly [impressed].
Xiao. ○ Master Fenshan of Jianmen was a native of Min. In his youth, he had attained personal realization regarding the Way, yet he eventually shaved his head and returned to his hometown.
People of the time called him a "mad monk," but Fenshan paid them no heed. He first met Lan’an Xu and later visited Miaoxi.

Upon hearing of his reputation at Shuangjing, [Dongshan] Fan determined that he would not allow him to enter the hall for practice. Consequently, Fenn, driven by indignation, descended the mountain intending to seek a way home.
He reached the banks of the Qiantang River and purchased a boat; standing still beside the Zhejiang Pavilion, he wept and said:
"I have come over these mountains with such toil and distress only to see Miaoxi, yet I am not even permitted to join the assembly. This must mean I lacked the Prajñā-pāramitā in my past lives."
It was a karmic condition. Suddenly, hearing the shout "Attendant coming! (Shilang lai), he attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse:
"For many years this matter has hung in my breast; I have questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened. Today my liver and entrails are suddenly rent asunder— A single cry:
'The Attendant comes upon the river! He returned directly to Yangyu and relied upon Layman An. Layman An certified his realization.
He attained [realization]. Before long, he suddenly took his leave. Lan’an sent him off with a verse, saying: "The wind is fierce at the riverhead and the flower-foam flies;
North and south they meet, yet no brow is unknitted. Only the hand of the refined and talented Chan-master Fen Casually snatches the embroidered banner and returns.
Thereafter, he feigned madness throughout Fujian. Sometimes he entered wine shops; sometimes he stayed among the fish markets. No one could fathom him, save for his companion...
Whenever Sanmuan Yong met him, he invariably treated him as his teacher. He once addressed the assembly, saying:
"Regarding this very plot of ground, you all—tell me, before heaven and earth were yet divided, where was it? Penetrate this directly."
"You have already been left behind by the Elder. If you further hesitate or deliberate, it will be more than a thousand or ten thousand miles away from the white clouds.
Suddenly he seized his staff, dispersed the assembly, and said: "Before the fifteenth day, all the stars in heaven bow toward the North;
after the fifteenth day, there is no water in the human world that does not flow toward the East. Previously...
Later, he set them all aside. "In every place, local dialects have different names," he said, and pointing his fingers, he bent them while counting:
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen. He then said again, "Brothers!"
Furthermore, tell me: what is today’s date? After a long silence, he said: "In our shop, we do not grant credit for even a single coin. Yian Quan was a native of Changhua in Lin’an.
He succeeded Wuan Quan and took up residence at Wannian Temple, where he remained for nine years.
His Dharma seat flourished greatly; nevertheless, Quan disciplined himself and served the assembly, ensuring that both his words and deeds were strictly regulated. For the most part, he emulated...
Regarding the person of Shui’an Cui of Fozhi: he constantly maintained an assembly of five hundred followers.
He had a self-eulogy that said: "My nose is like an eagle’s beak; it sees a thousand *li* before one's face. If you wish to recognize the Myriad Years, this very thing is it.

The monastic communities all loved him. Later, he moved to Huazang in Changzhou. At the beginning of the summer retreat, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Today, the mouth of the sack is tied shut. Tomorrow..."

O patch-robed monks, cease your aimless wandering! When the movements of the mind are extinguished, one can turn the body around. Even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar. In the sandalwood forest, let them gallop as they please;
raise the eyebrows and they sprout from the crown of the head. To gouge out flesh and create sores is to expose the family’s disgrace.
Both Emperor Gaozong and Emperor Xiaozong composed eulogies for the Great Being Maitreya. Among the practitioners of the Way in the monastic forests, there were none who did not harmonize with them;
yet few could satisfy the intentions of these two emperors. Their eulogy says: "A single cloud in the azure void; a solitary moon in the vast heavens."
Able to dwell beyond the mundane world—how wondrous and profoundly secluded! Habitually concealing himself within the marketplace—how extraordinary and heroic!
Accompanying him there is only his staff and his cloth bag; for satisfying hunger, what harm is there in wine, meat, and the scent of blood?

Parting, parting! The jade halls and crystal towers are further covered in snow. It is also said: "The bag contains heaven and earth; the staff carries the sun and moon. Rough and rugged, he is peerless among the sages."
Stoic and simple, a paragon among monks; for his commands, one blow leaves a trace of pain; to provoke the potential, one slap draws blood from the palm. Distinct! Distinct!
It is just like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace. During the Qiandao era, the Chan Master Zhidao resided at Baoning and once composed a verse in response:
"His capacity encompasses the great void; his eyes suspend the sun and moon. When he goes to the celestial palace, he is the sovereign within heaven."
Severed! Dwelling among men, he is the preeminent hero among men. Having cast down his cloth bag, he sits and cuts off the four great continents.
When he lifts up his staff, it causes the very earth to bleed. Farewell! Farewell! Though the principle is clear, it is difficult to vindicate.

Fan sent Li Gong to present a memorial to the Emperor. Emperor Xiaozong was greatly pleased and granted five hundred thousand coins and five hundred *hu* of rice to assist in providing for the assembly.
○ Bei-feng Yin moved from Jin-shan to Ru-peak. There was a physician named Lu An who, one night, dreamed of a divine being.
The response stated: "The Master is the reincarnation of Daguan Ying. By nature, the Master was leisurely and composed; he succeeded Huazang Min.
After departing from Sichuan, he went directly to Shuangjing to see Miaoxi. Miaoxi asked, "Where have you come from? Yinzong replied, "From West Sichuan."
Xiyun said, "Before you have even left Jian Pass, I shall give you thirty blows. Xianyin said, "It is right that you should rise for the Master.

Xiyun was lodged in the Laṅkā Hall and received very hospitable treatment from him. Later, he resided successively at various great monasteries. In his later years, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing, where he stayed for nine years.
He constantly used the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the basis for his Buddhist services. In the Gengchen year of the Shaoxing era, he passed away at Changpu Tian.
He took his leave of Tu-du at Ji-shan. Tu-du asked, "When will you depart, Master? Yin replied, "When the water reaches it, the channel is formed.

He then changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away. This was the eighth day of the twelfth month of that year. As he was about to depart, his disciples sought a verse from him. He wrote in large characters:
"A thousand verses, ten thousand verses—all are but feverish delusions. I have one phrase; after my death, let it be proclaimed. Tu-du... [text ends]
Tudu hurriedly carried the reliquary shrine back to the main hall of the Dharma. On the seventh day, he performed the funeral rites according to contemporary custom.

At that time, people were moved by his sincerity. Two years later, Tudu manifested his entry into nirvana. People harbored a heart of gratitude for his virtue. Tu Yin wrote of his reflections while in the mountains:
"In the forest, I am satiated with the sweet sleep of the single flavor; let the flames of worldly ambition blaze ever more fiercely, I shall not bring illness upon myself."

Seeking a cure for illness is mostly like trying to untangle a snare only to find more snarles added; one may have a coarse yam to eat like Lan Zan, yet lack even a single awl or table-leg like Xiangyan.

With the green mountains remaining by one's pillow, after the rain, layer upon layer of emerald drips from the eaves. Furthermore, I once composed a quatrain on the painting "The Peasant Drunk and Beating [the Earth]":
What cause has this peasant brought to harm the harmony of Heaven? Even after his drunkenness, he still beats the *rang* block as before.
Song: It was not like the drinking of Liu Bang and Xiang Yu in years past; In their breasts, each harbored his own spear and halberd.
When the Elder Tudu resided at Lake Jian, he was most intimate with Lu You (Fangong).

On the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month in the Renwu year of the Shaoxing era, the Elder passed away. Fangong lamented him in verse, saying: "The towering Dragon Gate has collapsed ten thousand fathoms high."

With graceful ease, his solitary figure travels west once more. Dust gathers upon his white whisk, and his corded meditation seat grows cold. Dewdrops fall upon the green pines as the egg-shaped stupa takes shape.
I imagine that his next rebirth will not be bound by the four great elements; we shall surely meet again in a third life. I, Fanglong, have deeply lacked spiritual cultivation;
I cannot help but feel the sorrow of parting from this mortal world. Furthermore, he praised his true likeness, saying: "His skeletal structure is exquisite and extraordinary; his spirit—"
He is carefree and elegant; his appearance is solemn yet harmonious, and his speech is exhaustive yet concise. Those who can capture him in painting find his heroic spirit overwhelming;
those who cannot do so possess but a single eye atop their heads.
Master Shichuang Gongchan traveled extensively to study under various masters. For a long time he relied upon Huanglong Zhong Daozhe, and later he relied upon Hongzhi.
During the Jingkang era, he returned from Huxiang to Dongyue. As he departed, Huanglong sent him off with this verse:

"Recalling idly those days of playing on the sandbars, Counting back on my fingers, forty autumns have passed since then. When you arrive at Shichuang, ask in leisure: 'How many winds [have there been]...'"
To whom did he pay his monthly dues? He respectfully emerged into the world to repay the kindness of his parents. Later, he resided at Ruiyan (Jewel Rock), where his Way flourished greatly.
Yet he lived with austere discipline for the sake of others, wearing plain cloth to withstand both cold and heat. Whether a matter was great or small, he would invariably attend to it personally.

The monastic community was brought into perfect order, and the practitioners submitted to him upon merely hearing his reputation. Once, on the Buddha’s birthday, he composed a verse which said: "A single tuft of *páng* grass from the Five Indias."
The "Mugwort Arrow" (Haojian): Stirring up the millions of soldiers of China, yet failing to carry out Yunmen’s true command; one nearly mistakes the markings on the scale of a balance.

This was widely circulated throughout the monastic forests, and there were those who attained realization even in their old age. A man from Sanqu, he and [Feng]gong both emerged from the lineage of Hongzhi.
His conduct was solitary and pure, and he did not associate with the world. He once served as the Guest Master at Taibai, where Miaoxi saw him.

He was exceptionally brilliant and quick-witted. I took pleasure in him and, using a stratagem, invited him to the Jade Couch (the imperial presence). However, Ch’ŏk’s resolve remained unshakable; he ultimately followed Old Tiantong.
At the beginning of the Qiandao era, [Master] Gong wished to recruit him to be his successor. He withdrew Ming from Bōn-am Temple and ordained him for public ministry.
He resided there for two years, and eminent masters from all quarters constantly sought refuge with him. Nevertheless, Ch’ŏk ultimately succeeded Hongzhi, not Gong.
Because he took no pleasure [in worldly things], Chè was likewise unconcerned. Later, he moved to Huazang in Wuzhou. As he was about to depart for his final journey, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
On his departure, he wrote this farewell verse: "A single phrase facing the sun, with no further detours or ambiguities. The moon sets in the cold pond; mist shrouds the ancient ferry."
He was one who truly attained the school of the Dongshan lineage; it is only a pity that he did not remain long in this world.

Emperor Xiaozong reigned for twenty-seven years. Whenever he summoned the elders of the various mountains to discuss the Way, it was only Chan Master Fozhao whom he held in the highest esteem and with whom he shared a deep mutual understanding.
At the beginning of the Chunxi era, while [Fozhao] was residing at Lengquan, the Emperor summoned him into Xuande Hall to engage in discourse on the Dharma.
Regarding the affairs of the Chan school, it has never been the case since antiquity that five successive nights were spent within the imperial palace. Thus, Fozhao once petitioned, saying:

"How have Your Majesty’s successive proclamations for the elders of the various mountains to discourse on the Way fared? Emperor Xiaozong replied: "It is rare to find anyone as direct and straightforward as these elders.
Fozhao further petitioned: "Your servant was raised among the mountain forests; my speech is coarse and crude. I humbly beg Your Majesty to be lenient [with me]."
[Lu] Dai. Emperor Xiaozong said, "It is perfectly fine for you to discuss the Way with this elder here, casting aside all worldly concerns.

Throughout his reign, the Emperor bestowed verses upon various mountain monasteries in no small number; those granted to Fozhao were the most esteemed. The Imperial words read: "In great heat, even metal and stone flow;
in cold winds, frozen clouds coalesce. The fragrance of plum blossoms drifts afar; there is naturally a springtime in a single branch. Fozhao once...
He harmonized with this. One day, he again issued an inquiry to Fozhao, saying: "The World-Honored One practiced the Way in the Snowy Mountains for six years;
what was it that he accomplished? I request that the Master explain this clearly. At that time, Fozhao was sitting at a lay patron’s house for a meal when the imperial messenger suddenly arrived.

He immediately requested to return and report. Fozhao composed his words and said: "I had thought Your Majesty had forgotten. This may be called the 'unconditioned spontaneity' that transcends a teacher."
This is wisdom.
○ Shui-an Yan was a native of Min. Initially, he studied under Miaoxi at the foot of Huigan Peak and thoroughly clarified the essential tenets of the school.
Miaoxi said, "This monkey will surely go on to trouble people in the future. Later, Yan took his leave of Miaoxi, composing a verse that begins: "Overturned..."
Riding an iron horse across the Xiao and Xiang rivers, the stream-side grasses and mountain flowers reveal themselves without concealment.

Having personally reached the summit of Mount Huíyàn, there is no further Buddha-dharma left to deliberate upon. Later, he resided at Longxiang on the riverbank, and many of his dharma brothers relied upon him.
Shuian composed a verse saying: "Now, upon the river, he has found the White-Browed One; for the sake of others, he uniquely employs the mechanism that cuts off the flow. Ran-yan was virtuous...
He composed verses. His "Eye of the School" was upright and correct. He inscribed the stone Buddha at Xīnchāng, saying: "Accumulating thoughts for many years, I gazed upon the stone Buddha;
Today, seeing it once, all doubt and suspicion are severed. Its face and features are simply like this— Yet they say it was carved out over three lifetimes.
He also inscribed the Dragon Pool (Lóngqiū), saying: "How could Jǐluò have cut off the Great Dragon Pool? His skillful means leave no path of error."
One sees only lofty crags and cascading waterfalls; who would know the serenity beyond the emerald ridges?
○ Bie Fengyun succeeded Shaoxi Jing. During the Chunxi era, he resided at Zhiti in Fuzhou; those seeking the Way throughout Jiang and Zhe all relied upon him.
He once composed a verse on Sudhana’s Southern Pilgrimage, which says: "The child with clearly parted hair."
"Wait until you hear of my belly's hunger; it will entice fifty-three spiritual friends. All their failures and shortcomings shall be brought back to him.
This was widely circulated throughout the monastic communities. Later, he moved to Huayan Temple in Fuyang, where he passed away.
○ Chan Master Hong was a native of Linchuan and succeeded Fozhao. He took up residence at Guangxiao Temple in Hongzhou in response to the command of You Yanzhi, the Commissioner of Grain Transport.

Subsequently, he served as the Prefectural Governor. During the morning and evening formal assemblies (*gongcan*), he required the abbots of various mountains to perform a long bow (*changyi*) beneath his official hall before withdrawing.
Upon hearing this, Hong was displeased, remarking that such a principle did not exist in the world, and immediately struck [the gong].
He beat the drum, ascended the hall, and retired from the monastery to depart. He spoke in verse: "The livelihood of the patriarchs was originally vast;
who would dare, in such a petty manner, bend their waist in servility? Cherish this well, O worthy Governor of Yuzhang; with straw sandals and bamboo staff, wander at ease as you please.

Upon hearing this, the Governor felt profound shame and sent an envoy to invite him again, but Hong never returned. From that time on, the various mountain monasteries of Jiangxi gained great prestige. Later—
The auspicious omen of Zhujia concluded with his relocation to Kaifu; the Vice Minister You Yanzhi personally composed a biography for him.
○ The monk Xuechao Yi styled himself a "village monk" and was a successor of Cudang Qing. He resided for a long time at Pingtian, later refusing an invitation from Changlu.
Only after reading Jiaoruihui’s memorial did he go there. The text of that memorial said: "A Buddhist monastery such as this is certainly no ordinary place..."
In this small grove, there is such a rustic monk; how could he be an ordinary blade of grass? To ensure that the gate matches the house, one must have a sublime environment and extraordinary people.
This man possesses an iron-like countenance and a reputation as vast as the heavens; were the entire world forged into a monastery, it would not suffice to fully manifest his teaching.
Were all the sands of the Ganges made into monks, they would not require even a single shout. Now, look!
The Bodhisattva Guanghuo (Flaming Light) turned his face away from the house of the Arhat Daoju, coming to support the bottomless boat and stirring up a thousand-foot wave of reeds.
One should cite the upward-pointing phrase: "May the Jade Leaves extend for ten thousand years.

Having already dwelt in the nest upon a single reed, the following year he returned to the Wan-nian [Monastery]. Not long after, he manifested his passing at Guanyin Yuan, first entering the coffin himself.
He locked the door and spoke a verse, saying: "This year I am seventy-five; I return to be the master of this hermitage. Be careful, Avalokiteśvara! A clay snake swallows a stone tiger.
Residing at Pingtian, his assembly was constantly five hundred strong. At that time, there was a mendicant from Ledu on Mount Tan in Jiangxi who was repairing the stupa of Daji (Mahāśīti).
His brothers all composed verses. Then, there was a presiding master (*upādhyāya*) who, having just changed his robes, entered the assembly and consequently completed [the verse].
A verse says: I send word to the old master of Jiangxi: Let him be roasted by the sun and fanned by the wind. It is not that his descendants lack the means to care for him;
He simply wishes to see the moment when the ice melts and the foundation crumbles. Furthermore, he wrote "On a Winter Day" as follows: The north wind understands the human heart as well;
It blows down the branches of the ancient tree before the cliff. Grant me a brazier of fire deep in the night, To turn [the pages of the scriptures].

Jiaoxin was lazy by nature and inclined toward idleness. Xuechao saw this and praised him greatly, saying, "A Chan practitioner who has spent thirty years in the assembly eating his meals might not necessarily produce such a work;
in the future, he will surely become a vessel of great capacity. Later, it indeed turned out as he had said.
Jiaoxin resided at Dongye and greatly promoted the teachings of the Nantai school; he is known as Master Shenzhao.
Once, while Songyuan was at Donghu, an official in charge of another temple requested a verse from him. Songyuan wrote in large characters: "The Yellow-Faced Gautama’s eyes are clouded with rheum;
He employs a thousand methods and ten thousand schemes to seek advantage. Now that there is no place for Wuzhuo to hide his whole body, He must have his descendants cover it over for him.
He showed this to the official, saying: "Whether speaking of Chan, speaking of the Way, or speaking of literary composition—when we meet as those beneath the forest, [we see this]."

How many times has he laughed? He has stepped upon the pivotal bolt of my house; that a man in white robes should become a Chancellor is but ordinary. Those of the lakes and seas recite this in competition.
○ Tanguangnan had long relied upon Miman; later, while in the assembly of Fozhao, he served as the head of the quarters (liaoyuan). He possessed transformative power.
The *Salt Verse* says: "Mixing water with mud and boiling them together in one place, when the mud and water are exhausted, the snow-flakes arise.
Thus one can demand the price of the distant heavens; the official seal is clear—who would dare dispute it? Fozhao said with delight, "This barbarian from Guangnan is truly vast.
Later, while residing at Daochang on Mount Xi, his Way was about to flourish when it was usurped by those in power. It did not last.
Ji. He passed away at Lengquan.
○ Leian received the position of Head Seat (Shouzuo). A native of Pingjiang, he possessed a dignified and imposing countenance.

Having long relied upon the various elders such as Yuedang and Rendang, he once compiled the *Pudeng* in thirty fascicles and also wrote commentaries on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. His hermitage was located at the Cao family hermitage in Xia. Together with...
The man of the Ping clan, a nephew of the layman Liu Jigao of Shushan, was most skilled [in this]. At the beginning of the Qianyuan era, Fucha (Fengxue Yanzhao) was at West Lake.
While Master Liu was serving in Danqiu, he invited him to Ba’en Temple on Zhongzi Peak. In response, Fengxue offered this verse of thanks:

"I have just finished building my thatched hut and am delighted to lean against the tall pines; With one pillow, the cool breeze, I sleep most soundly. As for the Way of Chan, there is nothing left to be understood."
When Liu was willing to enter the midst of the bustling crowd, Liu was greatly pleased and sent an envoy again to urge him. [Liu] also composed a verse in the same rhyme, saying:
"With a noble and towering physique leaning against the tall pines, In his later years, the cool shade is naturally deep. It is well to set foot for a while within the red dust;
What harm is there in being entirely amidst laughter and talk? In the end, he did not go. At that time, everyone held him in high esteem. Now, when one wags their tail...
"At a time of begging for pity, how could there still be such a person?

When Dàhuì was at Shuangjing, among his assembly of seventeen hundred "dragon elephants," there was a practitioner named Zǔqìng who, on the anniversary of his mother’s death, requested a verse from him.
Seeing that Zǔqìng’s bone structure was extraordinary, Dàhuì gave him this verse: "Passing through that one..."
Attached. Even the Buddha could not accommodate him. A fierce tiger sat blocking the road; the foxes and rabbits naturally hid their tracks.

In the year of Qingmiao, he appeared in the world at Nanyuan. He moved to Daolin Temple. One night, he dreamed that Master Baogong gave him twenty pairs of chopsticks. Upon waking, he did not understand the meaning.
At that time, Liu Shimu Hongfu was the military governor of Jinling and invited him to Mount Zhong. He resided there for two years.
Ten years later, it was rebuilt anew due to a fire. How could this have been a mere coincidence? At the beginning of the Qinyuan era, Fozhao returned from Wufeng to Yuyang;
subsequently, Qing succeeded him, only to pass away two years later. Thus, Miaoxi’s words proved to be unerring.
Master Huicang Guang succeeded Xuetang Xing and resided at Guifeng. He later moved to Fashi in Quanzhou at the command of Zhou Gui, the Minister of State Affairs.
At the time of his death, he entrusted a verse to his junior attendant Yuancong, saying:
"A poisonous seed in the monastic community—attendant Yuancong, you shall not endure my lineage; I shall extinguish your faction. Now I rest high upon my pillow, free from all worries."
When he heard of you, he struck the drum of lethal poison. Congjiu relied upon Mian for a long time and served as the head of the assembly at Mount Jing.
He appeared in the world at Ba’en in Hongzhou, then moved to Yunju, Yinjing, and Xuefeng. In his later years, by imperial decree, he resided at Mount Jing;
it was said that Huichan did not grant his approval lightly. Was this perhaps the lingering shade left behind by the compassionate practice of Xuetang?
○ When Yuanwu was first at a lecture hall in Chengdu, Chancellor Fan Bocai perceived that his character and substance were extraordinary.
He therefore composed a long poem to urge him to travel south on pilgrimage. The verse said: "In observing water, do not observe the water of a stagnant pond;
the fish and turtles of a stagnant pond are base. In ascending mountains, do not ascend a winding mountain; the winding mountain is but a place of weeds."
Muxi: To observe water, look directly at the vastness of the blue ocean; to climb a mountain, ascend straight to the summit of Mount Tai.

What is gained is no small thing, for what is seen is lofty. If you exhaust your efforts, it will not be in vain. Fortunately, there is a place in the south for the selection of Buddhas; you should strive within it to fathom the wondrous principle.
In years to come, having become a vessel of dharma, you shall restore the collapsing纲 (gāng). Do not fail the ambition of a man who has left the household life. Great Man!
O husband, cease your deliberations! How could you sacrifice your life for a hollow reputation? Moments of joy pass all too quickly;
yet time stealthily adds another year to our lives. Chengdu is indeed a city of great splendor, yet we have come to a halt because of the allure of fine wine.
My Master was originally one who has transcended the mundane; how could he be willing to follow the vulgar and sink into obscurity? My Master fortunately possesses the ambition of a rainbow;

do not let him waste his time mired in the mud and water. Have you not seen that a fish capable of swallowing a boat does not hide in a small stream, nor does a tree with a trunk as thick as two arms grow on Mount Danqiu?
When the Great Peng spreads its wings for ninety thousand li, would it ever fly like a swallow and settle upon the sand?
The gull—how can it compare to a galloping steed covering a thousand li in a swift current? Do not emulate the *jiaoliao* bird that clings to a single branch.

Even if you could expound upon a thousand sutras and treatises, you would still fall into the second level of the Chan school. White clouds naturally cherish the high peaks; shrouding them at dusk and morning, they do not open for even a moment.
Yet, to fulfill the hopes of the masses for rain, they emerge from the mountains quite casually. And have you not seen?
In the Jing Mountains there is jade named qióngyáo; though a skilled craftsman has not yet encountered it, it dwells amidst the weeds and brambles.
Had it not remained within the Jing and Chu regions at that time, how could its value have reached the "price of ten thousand cities," so many times higher?

Among the literati of our own land who have composed prefaces for the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of contemporary venerable masters, none have surpassed the three great elders—Shanggu, Wuwéi, and Wújìn—in the decisiveness and severance of their phrasing. In the present age, there is a man from Shu named Fēng Dāngkě.
He attained a profound mastery of the Chan school and composed a preface for the *Recorded Sayings* of Chan Master Huishui Huirong, which spread throughout the Jianghu region like a surging tide.
The text read: "In his later years, the Fifth Patriarch obtained Nantang, who was coarse, violent, and fierce; he overpowered Xiqin and Yuan.
Heaven was tight and earth was narrow. He threw himself upon the Great Sui, saying that the Way-master possessed the hand of one who strikes stone with a hammer, striking upward at the firm."

Tall and imposing, his strength was coarse; with a single blow, he would pierce through. Returning to sit atop Mount Diaoyu, he was ten times more formidable than his master—his rugged cliffs were steep and precipitous, and his fierce poison was such that no one could bring themselves to taste it. His disciple Yanwen did not even glance at it;
wishing to collect the remaining venom and distribute it throughout all quarters, I fear that later people might fail to heed the benefit and instead meet their own downfall. Therefore...
To mark its bitter poison and show it to those who come after, this preface was written by the rustic old man of Jin-yun.
The Layman Wu-gou, Zhang Jiu-cheng, studied under Miaoxi and attained great awakening; his insight into the essence of the school became clear and lucid.

"Try this: it is old and yet even greater. As for the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, totaling over eighty-four thousand fascicles—when they reach the face of this fellow, they do not even require a single spittle.

The ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment—when they reach the face of this fellow, they do not even merit a single glance. For many years, like ripened fruit, he has raised five tigers."
My son, you have traveled across the four seas, casting excrement and spitting filth into the lands of the Great Tang,
Japan, and Silla, until the heavens and earth were plunged into darkness, the sun and moon rushed in frantic haste, Mount Sumeru trembled in its foundations, and the four oceans surged with waves.
With a haughty air, he strikes the strings and pipes; let us take a brief seat and observe him.

His countenance and features are as coarse as those of a peasant boy from a village of three households, yet his functioning is like a dark wind and black rain, amidst the thunder, lightning, and the roar of a clap of thunder.
Amidst the clattering of the double-reed oboe, he drags away a great, raging fire. *Du!* What idle business is this?
Jiangshan Yuan succeeded Ciming. Yuan later obtained Xuedou Ya; Ya obtained Cijue Yin. Ran inherited [the lineage] through a process of harmonious fusion.
During the Qiandao era, Ran resided at Tianxi in Jinling, while Miaochi Chan resided at Baoning.
Mingda resided at Jiangshan. Mingboran [criticized him], asserting that his lineage was not a direct descendant of Huanglong and Yangqi.

He once engaged in a formal debate with him; however, Mingboran was eloquent and quick-witted, and Mingda was somewhat outmaneuvered by him. Ultimately, Mingboran understood the meaning of "Dumb Chan" (Chichan).
However, his capacity and caliber surpassed those of others; it was simply that he appeared in the world too early and did not travel through the various monastic lineages.

Consequently, the doctrinal eye became muddled, and for this reason, many in the monastic communities disparaged him. Later, he resided at Nanhua and passed away in Wuyang. As he departed, he displayed a spirit of liberation and detachment.
The people of the state piled up *kukubh* incense to cremate him; this was a singular excellence of no small measure.

I share the same karmic affinity with Enshō, yet I regret not having had the opportunity to know his compassionate model. I most cherish his essay on the memorial service for Chikaku; it is truly excellent. It says:
In the third year of the Jianyan era, I suddenly became strange and eccentric. I took off my head-wrap, fastened my waist-belt, and at night stole into the Master’s courtyard.
There I was caught and defeated by the Master. Since I had nothing with me, I simply prostrated three times. From that time on, I withdrew in reflection, regretting that my offense was not small.

If someone reviled the Master, saying, "This old fellow is not clever at all; he has no ability to explain anything," I would immediately raise my head, looking up at heaven in celebration and wonder.

If someone praised the Master, saying, "His Way transcends the Buddhas and Patriarchs; his capacity is as vast as the ocean," I would immediately take up my staff and strike him until his head was shattered.

"How is it? How is it?"—many have misunderstood this. I respectfully present these meager offerings. The Master laughed heartily. Now, there was a junior disciple named Daji who, during the Chunxi era, resided at Lingyao in Quzhou.
At that time, the imperial court was implementing the labor service system (*yifa*), and quotas were being assigned across the two Zhejiang provinces and the Huai region.
Daji then organized and led the monks, nuns, and Daoists of the three prefectures of Qu, Wu, and Chu to... [construct the stupa].
The Emperor granted him an exemption from labor service in the morning; thus, the monks and Daoists throughout the realm obtained peace.

That they were not subjected to the corvée duties of the state was surely due to the power of [Master] Ji. Those who wear the shaven head and the square robe in the future should know their origins therein.
After Ji, he resided at Pingtian on Mount Tiantai and passed away.
Kengtang Chong met Wan’an Yan; his nature and understanding were sharp and keen, and he was broadly versed in matters of antiquity and the present.
He composed a great many words and phrases throughout his career. Among them was a preface he wrote for the *Record of Master Qiandiu*, sent by a monk on a visit to Layman Jianchu You Shiliao.
The text reads: "Under the mountains of Min and E, there dwells a tiger of the Three Corners. Leaping into the South, who dares to insult him? Le..."
Old Tan aimed his eyes and released a flash of light; with his back turned, he secretly loosed a crossbow of a thousand-jun strength.
A single arrow struck the mark, reviving the dead; from then on, the fangs used for biting were never revealed. For forty years in Mount Wuning, how could he have merely cut off the road of Jiangxi?
When Tudu of Jing Mountain met that one mouthful, even now there is no way to clear his name. He instead sent his disciple away...
Vipa asked after the layman, seeking a turning word. When the layman praised him, his mouth immediately became mute;
when the layman reviled him, his eyes immediately became blind. Regarding that which lies beyond both praise and revilement, I request you to compose a preface for his *yulu* (recorded sayings).
Gongan Shu was a native of Chuang. He also succeeded Wanzan as his dharma heir. By nature he was upright and outspoken; no one could win him over or alienate him.
During the Qiandao era, he traveled through the regions of Huxiang. He once offered this self-eulogy: "Moonlight illuminates the mountain valleys; the sound of spring water falls upon the precipice.
Amidst the colors of water and mountains, there lies a single piece of rotten, withered firewood. He also said: "An old crane enters a dried-up pond; it understands well..."
Sheathed feathers and wings; a single dot upon the back, soaring to the heavens. The world within the pitcher is narrow.
○ Shun of Ruiyan succeeded Shui’an and was titled Weitang. Initially at Meishan in Chi, he once gave a discourse on the occasion of ascending the hall, saying:
"Today is the fifteenth day of the fifth month; last night it rained incessantly. I do not know how the practitioners beneath the forest trees perceive it."
When meeting someone, how do you bring it up? If you can bring it up completely, there is a fist that strikes across the chest and splits the face. Why is it so?
"If refined gold does not pass through the furnace and smelting, how could its brilliance emerge with such thorough radiance? Furthermore:

"Ten days in the inner chamber, five days ascending the hall—thousandfold uglinesses and hundredfold clumsinesses, nowhere to hide them. *Du!* (A shout) You are dragged together into the boiling cauldron. He passed away later at Tai.
Ruian. ○ Wanshou Xiu was a native of Min. Initially he relied upon Ying’an; later he met Huo’an at Wuxi in Changzhou.
He entered the world at Shangfang in Xie and subsequently moved to Shuangta. His Way had not yet flourished, so he traveled from Tudu Ziji to Nengren.
Carrying his alms bowl, he passed through the Wu Gate. A group of virtuous friends invited him for a small discourse (*xiao can*). As the attendant led him to his seat, he said:
"The treasury of the true Dharma eye was extinguished at the side of this blind donkey; it has reached the point where all the people of the great earth cannot support it.

For this reason, thorns and brambles reach the heavens along the road to Caoxi, and skulls cover the fields before the peak of Shaoshi. It would take no one but Lu or Bian [the legendary physicians] to raise them up."

For a malady as deep-seated as that of the gallbladder and diaphragm, none but those of the Sun and Wu schools can fully master the mechanism of killing and enlivening. A single blow of the poisoned drum causes all who hear it to perish;
when the vital ford is seized and cut off, a new spirit and bone arise. Since there are such masters as these, the Buddha-dharma need not fear being allowed to rot.
Nevertheless, even so, tell me: when one drops one’s arms while walking along the path, how does one utter the single phrase that universally illuminates all capacities?
The Way has arisen. Three feet of numinous light; the command of Makara. The whole city is filled with harmonious qi, warm as spring.
[He] descends from his seat. Tudu grasps his hand and says: "I thought that after Hui'an there was no one else; it turns out my nephew is here.
From this point on, the Way shall be practiced in the Wu region."
Xia’an Wuzhu was a native of Changshu in Suzhou. He renounced secular life to become a monk. Initially, he studied under Wuan Quan;
later, he studied under Mian Shanbao at Wugu in Quzhou. During the Chunxi era, he led the assembly at Lengquan, making exclusive offerings his primary concern.
At a time of great famine, while Mian Shanbao had not yet returned from holding his alms bowl and the administrative officials were restricting access, Wuzhu sat in meditation.
The mountain gate was opened and he was admitted according to the usual custom. When Mitan returned, the administrative officials (zhishi) tried to dissuade him;
seeing that Miyan’s expression seemed displeased, they took their leave. Miyan remarked, "I only require a cloister as large as a hand-span to provide full offerings for monks from the five lakes.
Not long after, he resided at Xiangfu in Quzhou and subsequently managed several monasteries, truly making the provision of offerings his primary concern.
Master Kumu Yuan of Yanshan, a successor of Miaoxi, presented this verse to the assembly: "The dry wood of Yanshan is true Zen;
It does not reside in clever or novel phrases. When one suddenly grasps it with hands behind one's back, The great whale swallows the moon and the waves overflow the heavens."
Baoshou of Mount Gui also succeeded Dahui. A veteran of the monastic community, he lived late in life at Da Mei.
He had a verse that said: An eighty-year-old old man rolls a brocade ball; Rolling it on and on, he does not know when to stop. Now he rolls it toward the crest of a thousand peaks.
Sitting and watching the water-buffalo of Mt. Huai. ○ Kōng Tōzan (Empty Dongshan).

Fú Rén (Fukun) first met Cǎotáng Qīng (Sōtō Seiryū); later he met Miàoxī (Myōkaku). When Miàoxī saw that his bearing and spirit were transcendent and outstanding, he wished to "entrap" him [as a disciple].
He brought him before him and offered a verse of praise for his *dingxiang* (crown-mark), saying: "Huìkōng has grasped my itchy spots; I..."
I have once pricked him where it hurts. Where it hurts, there is an itch; where it itches, there is pain. This does not share the path with the thousand sages;
how could it be shared by patch-robed monks? Who knows that within the bamboo of the broom there is no money-tube, and within the thickets of mugwort there are no beams for a hall?
Nowadays, each person is unaware of themselves, leaving it to others to paint such incompetent, old, frozen sores as these.
Let them hang in the corners of walls; let them burn *turuṣka*, *bhallātaka*, and *agaru* resin incense day and night as offerings to their ancestors for seven generations.
Yet, though they hold their vows in vain without wavering, they ultimately inherit only the "Grass Hall" (Cóngtáng) lineage.

Among those with discernment in the forest [of Chan], all looked up to him with admiration. Xingkong was skilled at composing verses; his *Dongshan Waiji* (Supplementary Collection from Dongshan) circulates in the world.

For instance, he said: *Dongshan’s parting words to someone were but a single phrase:* *"Just as you are about to receive my respect, I shout and send you out."* *"Now, seeking further on paper—this is much like a fierce hawk seizing a fox or a hare."* *"Master, Master, do you know or not?"* *It is truly so.*
Sitting and waiting for it, there is no end in sight. Seize the autumn wind while the frost makes the trees fall. Lestan (Lectan) and Baizhang were in Jiangxi;
there was one named Shengcishan who dwelt in a secluded cliff, and his *Lukong* (Carving the Void) collection circulated throughout Jiangzhe.
Regarding the practice of using the name of one’s hermitage or hall as a monastic title (*dào-hào*), there was no such precedent among the predecessors;

rather, they were addressed simply by the location where they resided, such as Nanyue, Qingyuan, Baizhang, and Huangbo. As for the term "An" (Hermitage) or "Tang" (Hall), it originated with Chan Master Baojue Xin, who retired from his duties at Huanglong and dwelt in seclusion at Huītáng;
consequently, people came to address him by that name. Subsequently, Lingyuan, Sīxīn, and Cāotáng all followed this same practice.
They were eminent disciples; therefore, they successively emulated one another. Zhenjing and Huitang both emerged from the school of Huanglong, and thus he was also addressed by the title Yun'an.
Juefan was the spiritual son of Yun'an, and thus he designated himself with the titles Jiyin and Ganlumei.
Generally speaking, dharma names are either invoked based on one's given name or designated according to one's birthplace or place of residence.

As for those who establish [a name] based on attaining realization through diligent practice, and those who propagate it based on the path they abide in, both have prior foundations to rely upon; how could this be a matter of mere casualness?

Yet, the brothers of today, as soon as they enter the assembly, even before they have dreamed of the "one stroke" that points beyond, already each establish a dharma-name, showing no regard at all for...
To trace its origin: During the summer retreat, Zen Master Xiatang Yuan asked the administrative official, "How many fans have been distributed this summer?
The official replied, "About five hundred handles. Yuan said, "Then another five hundred huts must be built.
This was because whenever a monk received a handle for a fan, he would invariably write a name for a hut upon it. Those who heard this were all greatly amazed.
Xiao. My mother dreamed of a Buddhist monk with a full moon atop his head who entered her embrace; upon waking, she raised me as her child.

If it is not like this at all, then how is it? "Without entering the startling waves, it is difficult to encounter a fish to one's heart's content.
It is also said: "The precious sword is never lost; the empty boat is never carved. In the morning one roams Mount Luofu; in the evening one returns."

Dantideva, if you claim that this is the land of primordial radiance, it would logically have to be so; yet this is precisely like one sitting in a well gazing at the sky, or using a conch shell to measure the ocean.
To claim that "speech is not sound" and "form is not matter" is not only to be confused about the fundamental tenets, but also to lose the essential meaning.
If one wishes to clarify the essential meaning of the school, what then? "Secretly embroidering the mandarin ducks at leisure; let others seek the golden needle for themselves.
Chan Master Zu Zhao Changlu (Duohe), a native of Putian, first traveled to the capital carrying his book-bag. There was a high-ranking eunuch...
Seeing that his appearance and character were extraordinary, [the official] offered him a Buddhist ordination certificate (*duò*). Huihe would not accept it, saying to his fellow students:
"I am a great man; how could I ever fall beneath another's eunuch? If I were to accept his favor for even a single day, I would be bound by it for the rest of my life.
Fortunately, our Buddha has vast Dharma gates, and the state has opened up a path for men."
"I shall exert myself. With such resolute intent, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and, within that same year, passed the scriptural examination to receive ordination as a *bhikṣu*.
He traveled extensively throughout various regions before eventually residing at Changlu, where his assembly was constantly filled with over a thousand followers.

When Zhenxie Le arrived from the assembly at Danxia, he was still quite young; however, Huihe, seeing his quick-wittedness and sharp intelligence, appointed him as the head of the community. Later, he retired from the monastery.
He was about to bestow it upon him, intending for him to be his successor. When he reached for the robe, [the Master] said: "I received the Dharma in the chamber of Danxia;

the robe was transmitted in the courtyard of Zuozhao. The kindness is so deep that words fail; what is held in the heart is naturally clear. Hezi did not take pleasure in this; he descended from his seat and seized the robe back.

From that time forth, he never again donned the dharma robes for the rest of his life; in the end, he succeeded Danxia Chun. Among those with discernment throughout the rivers and lakes, all praised him for not forgetting his origins.
Oran addressed the assembly, saying: "In the early years of the Shaoxing era, my physical strength was robust. Wherever I went, I would part the weeds to behold [the truth]..."

Feng saw a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who, with his bag suspended and his alms bowl hanging from his belt, beat his hands in rhythm and struck the gate of realization; he forgot to eat and neglected his sleep, never ceasing even at the break of dawn.
Furthermore, he encountered a great man and a wise master who, tireless from morning until night, used bitter words to transform him and prodded him like a sharp awl.

Yet, even then, he could not gather up his old wares nor bring them into his own hands. How much more so in the present age, when those who occupy positions in the monasteries everywhere are merely practitioners of Chan!
As for the Master, he merely occupies a name; his ascending the hall and entering the room serve only as a token that he is not empty.

When the master sees the student and the student sees the master, they fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, becoming muddied by one another’s confusion. What more need be said of a single word or half a phrase?
Transcending ordinary sentiments, one reaches the great ground of non-doubting peace and bliss. Having snapped the binding ropes, one pierces the nostrils of all people under heaven.

The Great Way is on the verge of extinction; yet there are still those who carry their books in baskets and their staffs upon their shoulders, seeking refuge beneath the smoke and flames of human habitation.
For the most part, they seek only fullness, warmth, and comfort; they dabble in non-Buddhist classics merely to provide material for conversation.

Regarding the fundamental matters of the True Dharma, they remain silent and do not discuss them. Furthermore, those who occupy monastic seats and aspire to prominent temples rely on their karmic fortune to attend upon high-ranking officials and cultivate relationships with the noble as external protectors.
Having thus devised a plan for their own convenience, this has eventually become a prevailing custom that is passed down from one to another.

Imitating [others], there are few who recognize their error. Among them, even those who are authentic "yellow-faced old monks" (bhikṣus), though they may have realized the fruits of the Way and secretly pursued the ancient style, remain withdrawn and hidden, maintaining their humble station.
They cannot draw near to those in power, nor do they have the strength to remedy prevailing abuses.
Sitting solemnly in a cold place with hands folded in one’s sleeves, one can only imagine them nodding in sighing admiration at these various trivial and desolate skills. I pray—
Having attained the true cause for possessing the eye of wisdom, you who are men of superior capacity must exert yourselves with vigorous introspection. Aim for the distant rather than the near;
within your own person, discern the wondrous mystery that has not been transmitted from the West, and deploy the unfathomable mechanisms that transcend both the ordinary and the sage.
In days to come, serve as a model for future generations, so that you may avoid the lamentation of being a solitary wanderer on the road for a thousand li. Be clear!
Before these people, I have laid bare my innermost thoughts. I also hope that you will take the declining state of the ancestral Way to heart and leap with joy beyond the six realms of existence.
It is precious that you, O brilliant patch-robed monks, shall bring illumination to the world, so that beneath ten thousand ages, the Diamond King’s precious sword remains majestic and undiminished.
When Dongpo arrived at Jingkou, Foyin crossed the river to pay his respects. Dongpo said, "In the past, Zhaozhou did not descend from his meditation seat;
why has Jinnshan today crossed the river? Foyin replied with a verse: "Zhaozhou in the past lacked the light of humility, Not descending from his seat to receive the Two Kings.
How can he compare to Jinnshan’s immeasurable marks, Which encompass the sands of the great trichiliocosm?"
The *dhātu* (elements) are the meditation couch.
○ Master Zeng Wenqing was a native of Ganzhou; he was the younger brother of Minister Baowen Tianyou and had made significant progress in the Chan school.
He was a spiritual friend (*fangwai you*) of Chan Master Xinwen Ben. Once, regarding the World-Honored One holding up a flower—
Verse: Many on the rivers and lakes admire this. The verse says: "Plucking up a flowering branch for all to see— Kāśyapa, for no reason, broke into a smile.
From this moment, the spring light was entirely leaked forth; Peaches red and plums white fill the world.
Furthermore, he praised the image of Xinwen (Heart-Hearing), saying: "This is Old Xinwen: silent and without sound. This is not Old Xinwen: his form is solemn and present. Look at him!"
It is not non-existent; listen to it as being not existent. One who can contemplate in this way is not one who hears with the mind.
The Dharma Master Lingying Fajing of Wuzhou was encroached upon in his monastic affairs by late learners.
He petitioned Prime Minister Ye for assistance. Prime Minister Ye replied in a letter, saying: "I have received your earnest letter through your special envoy; I know that you and I..."

Regarding our prior karmic connection, we share the same neighborhood and hometown. Upon inquiring among my fellow practitioners, I learned that you are a man of fundamental integrity who has resided at Lingying Temple for forty years.
You have transformed a field of rubble into a magnificent edifice, ensuring that the sound of the fish-shaped drum and the wooden gong does not cease even in the late years.
It may be said that you are truly willing to provide offerings and exert your physical strength within the temple grounds to bring this precious hall to completion.
At that time, he gave rise to a mind of greed and delusion toward the junior monks who had violated their precepts, devising clever schemes to seize [the property].

He resented that the Master could not bring his supreme undertaking to completion. If one were to judge this by worldly standards, it would be truly unbearable for a magpie’s nest to be occupied by a pigeon.
However, if one views it from the Master’s own perspective, his body is not his own, and all phenomena are like dreams and illusions; thus, his spirit—
Should this site of practice not also be your long-term livelihood? Thus the ancients said: "When staying, one is like a solitary crane perching coldly atop a pine;
when departing, one is like a fragment of cloud suddenly passing over the human world. In going and staying, one is unencumbered; how could there be any obstruction?
One must abide while never being one who does not abide; only then will one know oneself to be a person who both goes and stays.

Furthermore, since every sip of drink and every morsel of food is predetermined from before, whether one moves or stops, how could it be a matter of human agency? Do not harbor intentions regarding necessity, certainty, identity, or difference.
If you cannot see through this realm with total clarity and lucidity, then at the final moment, you will inevitably be mired in the mud.
Water. Departing from here, it would be well to sit unmoving within a bright window beneath a green pine tree and settle the great matter of your own house.
Such an opportunity is truly a stroke of fortune. If you wish to borrow a single word from me, O Five-Horse Official, there is the difficulty of lifting up mountains and leaping over the sea;
yet if you can awaken to the fact that all phenomena are empty, for you there will be the ease of transforming the mundane into the sacred. If this is not yet so, [it will remain difficult].
"Quickly prepare your pack! Hurry to visit his new bride. Hunyuan Mi was a native of Tai.
He was a successor of Guishan Guang Zhuangyuan. By nature he was poor, yet he maintained his integrity and did not boast of himself.
When he moved from Fushan to Dasheshan, his path passed by his lay relatives' home. He intended to see his brothers and kinsmen, and thus instructed his attendants:
"Follow me, but do not go beyond his house; bring only one or two close attendants with you.
He further said, "If you see my elder brother, do not utter a sound or respond at all, for I fear it might startle the people of the village. Such was his consideration. There is a verse that says:
"Having taken refuge and come to this thatched hut, The three rafters are planted not deep. How could this lowly and humble body Yet understand the sound of a rolling thunder? He sowed the millet.
"No beans grow there; picking up lead, it is indeed gold. It is only because of a misstep that one ultimately does not fall into hesitation.

The monastic communities all acknowledged his discernment as lofty and far-reaching. How can he be compared to those who falsely claim the names Zhang, Wang, Li, or Zhao? They are not of the same day!
Therefore, the Director-General Jien Gong Longwen composed a memorial for Longxiang, requesting Master Mi, saying: "Thirteen men have passed through the barrier of Yangyu;
you were first among them as their leader. For two thousand li you pursued the alms-bowl of Huangmei; Master Mi was right by your side."
It may be said that the True Dharma has been duly received. You, a public official, have selected this humble individual; your footing is firm and your vision is clear.

You have raised the purple sheath to expound the Chan of great blessings, such that all quarters look up to you with mountain-like reverence. Having crossed the Stone Bridge, you carry the almsbowl of the Seven Min Provinces, followed by ten thousand monks like gathering clouds.
For it was here that the Six Dragons once reigned in the Central States; thus, these two circuits of Zhejiang alone boast their preeminent monasteries. Next, it is appropriate...

As a successor to the Dharma seat, you should not remain on the solitary islet alone; rather, dwell between the two peaks. Let the *huatou* be present everywhere; a single phrase encompasses the three essentials.
With the eyes of the assembly turned toward you in unison, you were subsequently commanded by imperial decree to reside at Jingci Temple on West Lake.
