Master Cien was the son of General Wei Chi of the Tang dynasty. When he was ten years old, he was already capable of composing military strategies;

his father esteemed him for this. Xuanzang, desiring that he leave the household life to pursue the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), secretly stole the strategies he had composed and taught them to a novice monk to recite.
He took the boy to visit Wei Chi, who praised his son’s excellence with great fervor.
He was able to compose a literary work. Kumārajīva asked to see it and remarked, "This kind of composition even a young novice boy could recite.

He called the boy over immediately; when the boy recited it, there was not a single character out of place. Kumārajīva was greatly enraged, thinking the boy was mocking him with archaic texts, and he intended to execute him on the spot.
Master Kumārajīva interceded, saying, "The Buddha has taught that he protects and saves all sentient beings. If you do not..."

"Save me! I am no longer a disciple of the Buddha. It would be better for you to abandon me and leave the monastic life; what do you think? Xuanzang followed this advice and thereby obtained [the horse].
He was immediately ordained as a *bhikṣu*, and none among the assembly could surpass him. He frequently lectured and debated before the Emperor, who bestowed upon him a jade ring.

Upon seeing the Son of Heaven, he no longer performed the ritual prostrations; instead, whenever he entered or departed, three carriages accompanied him—carrying scriptures and treatises, wine and food, and women.
Lord Xuan wore his robes and was suspicious of him; the Dharma Master also disparaged the Lesser Vehicle and doubted the account of the divine offerings.
One day he visited Lord Xuan specifically to seek the celestial provisions. They conversed all day long, yet no such offerings were seen.
After the Dharma Master returned home, when he first arrived, Lord Xuan rebuked him, saying, "Why have you arrived at an improper time? The spirit informed him, "It is not because of negligence."
Today, the Master engaged in discussion with a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva; a ray of light enveloped him, pervading the entire realm, such that no path could be found to enter it.
From this moment on, I have further inclined my heart to revere him. Thus one knows that what the Mahāyāna contains cannot be fathomed by those of inferior faculties.
Dun’an Yan was a native of Min. Initially, he studied under Yuan Kumu; later, he attended Miaoxi at Mount Jing.

Together with Zu’ān Yin and Tong’ān Lián, he compiled the *Extensive Record of Dahui* in thirty fascicles, which circulated widely throughout the world. After Dahui passed away, Yan no longer traveled abroad.
Wearing a single robe through both cold and heat, he remained in one place for thirty years. He served as the head of the printing workshop several times in Min.
When the General Zhao Ruyu invited him to Mount Xiufeng in Fuzhou, he lay firm in his refusal and would not rise. Biéfēng composed a memorial to exhort him, containing the lines:

"In the forest of the hidden orchid, how could it be that there is no fragrance when people are absent? Within the Way of the ultimate treasure, it is only when one possesses the discerning eye that it is first recognized.
At the time, everyone praised his pure integrity. In his later years, he was ultimately subjected to the "poisoned paint" and driven out.

In the Flower Treasury of the Eternal, he sat for nineteen years. The Dharma assembly flourished throughout the Three Wu regions; this was simply because his karmic conditions found their ground there.
○ Zu’ān Yin was a native of Chu’an. Initially he relied upon Jishì, and later he attended upon Dàhuì. He emerged from seclusion at Hélín in Jīngkǒu.
He praised himself, saying: "My body is frail and worn; I shall act with humble simplicity. With hands folded in solemnity, one may know the propriety of ritual.
Whether beauty or ugliness comes, I do not judge it myself; I entrust the wandering of my path to looking down upon it."
The Prince of Yingyang initially resided in Jiahe, where his official rank had not yet been attained and his family estate was in decline.
At that time, Chan Master Shui'an Cui was residing at Ba'en Temple; he and the prince were close associates, and there was no doubt the master did not resolve for him.

When Emperor Xiaozong ascended the throne, the prince successively governed several great provinces and appointed Master Cui to preside over many famous monasteries throughout the various regions. Toward the end of his life, [the prince] requested...
He designated which mountain was to be Gongde Temple and also appointed Cui to preside over it, granting him a special purple robe.
Zen Master Yuanwu and his descendants likewise served as a bulwark for the Great Dharma; it is said that they came here through the power of their mutual great vows.
The Great Affairs of the Forest Monasteries (Concluded).
In the past, when I was at the head of the assembly at Wufeng, the Chan Master Guyu Rong actually held the office of Chief Attendant (*kangyin*).

Having had the honor of serving alongside him, I accompanied him daily for several years, enjoying the pleasures of mountain and stream. Subsequently, due to karmic conditions, I came to reside at Qingshan.

It has been more than ten years since he last visited. One day, he arrived at my place with effortless grace. During our conversation, he spoke at length about the deeds and words of the past, which greatly refreshed his venerable mind.
He then gradually produced a volume titled *The Great Events of the Forests*, containing the exchanges and poetic compositions between world-renowned patriarchs and worthy scholar-officials.
These truly serve to admonish later students and supplement the religious teachings; for the most part, they are consistent with—
This work is similar to that of my late teacher Wuku; it is likely to be carved onto woodblocks to benefit future generations. How vast will its benefit not be!
Thus, I have taken up my brush to inscribe this at the end. Postscript by Zongyan of Huizang Dun’an, Jinyun Jiwu (1219).
Rong saw Tu-du Ce; Ce saw You-dian Niu. He was the sixth-generation descendant of Huanglong (these eighteen characters appear next in the later ancient edition).
The newly carved *Conglin Shengshi* (Great Events of the Forests) compiles records from the *Yalu*, *Jitan*, and up to the works of Kuya of Siming.

It gathers the hidden practices and subtle mechanisms of ancient Buddhas and patriarchs, as well as the matters concerning Chan and Buddhism shared by worthy gentlemen that were disclosed in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*. This is bequeathed to future generations. Its...

This is for the sake of the Dharma-gift, so that those who are latecomers may tread the path and know the way of upward entry, rather than merely serving as material for the talking-sticks of today’s superficial lecturers.
Furthermore, regarding the flourishing events of the monastic community under Master Rong of Danqiu during the Song dynasty, every word and every phrase is an iron-clad case for all eternity;
his Chan and his Way serve as a great standard and mirror. Yet, the Song edition has long since been lost.
Lacking a reliable basis for ancestral transmission, this work exists in various locations throughout the land.

Hidden within Zen quarters, it has been transcribed with errors as grave as those of "Hai" and "Zhi," leading to successive generations perpetuating mistakes and corruptions until, ultimately, no complete edition remains.

Now, the lay practitioner Wusheng of Dongwu Yuan, intending to pass through the nostrils of the former sage Zhixu and seize him during his confession, happened upon the auspicious discovery of an ancient manuscript. He has thus enabled me to verify and examine it.
It was printed once and circulated throughout the world; indeed, his resolve to protect the school and defend the Dharma was profound.

Having thus collated and reviewed these materials, I divided them into two fascicles and entrusted them to the carvers. Some may say: "What benefit do such Chan records provide to the Chan monasteries of today?
There is a certain class of Chan practitioners who employ ornate prose and embellished phrasing merely to match the level [of conventional literature]."
Birth and transcendence of the world lead to advancement in the monastery; these serve as the ladder and the medium. Until death, do not allow even a single thought to arise.

Upon a dry piece of dung, one may practice by taking up the three sutras and five treatises, treating the doctrinal systems of the Tiantai and Huayan schools as identical to the "critical phrases" (huatou) of the patriarchs.
Furthermore, you claim that Deshan and Linji ascended to which of the ten stages of the Three Sages, and that Zhaozhou and Yunmen attained which of the six levels of "realization" (*jijue*).
Such a concoction of forced syntheses attempts to subsume Chan within the Teachings (*jiao*). But what form does Chan actually take? What Chan is there to investigate?

Yet one must consider that the Patriarch came from the West to transmit the Single Dharma-door, pointing directly to the human heart. Even these [doctrinal] explanations are merely texts for the substance of the Teachings.

This body is but a redundant finger or a fleshy tumor. Thus, for those who practice Chan today, it would be better to relinquish their Chan seats and robes and instead be registered as the servants of a *zuoshouzhu* (a presiding master).
How lamentable! The words and phrases of the ancient Way and the Patriarchs accorded with the *Sūtras*, and a single shout could penetrate all five teachings;
these are utterly different from the biased interpretations of today. Little do they realize this.
Within the gateway of the Buddha-dharma, there is a single path of life. The tongues of the ancient sages possessed a distinct point of landing.

Furthermore, there is a certain class of monastics who, having been endowed with a seemingly perfect disposition from their youth, possess the "ghost-eye" of silent illumination; for a lifetime they carry a single board, using the "beyond-the-teachings" (kiao-wai) as a pretext.

They have no desire to contemplate the "half-character" (the provisional teachings), yet they do not fail to observe the rules of Chan meditation. They do not know what their fundamental mastery is like;

though they do not carry the Dharma on their bellies as others do these days, they claim that the Buddha-dharma is far too easy. They stubbornly cling to the manifest, flowing consciousness, taking this to be their own true portion.
I hope that none among you who have not yet lost their humanity will recklessly slander the ancient sages, mistake a servant for a lord, or harbor arrogance within themselves.
Do not resort to the manipulation of strange wonders to delude men and women, teaching them to fall into the perilous pits of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
Unless one is utterly illiterate, they should not presume to be a "Chan practitioner" or a "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra); as for all others, this is not the case.
May we avoid the lament of the "cold cicada clinging to the wood" and the ridicule of the "rotten winter melon in one hall.

Furthermore, there is another class of shaven-headed donkeys who cultivate connections with princes and lords, practicing sycophancy toward patrons; their frantic pursuit of fame and profit knows no bounds, reaching even its ultimate excess.
Thus, they have discarded their former cultivation and rely entirely upon the permanent endowment. They treat the *caitya* (the temple) as a shop, sweeping away all sense of shame and integrity.
Seeking profit and greedily coveting goods, they take their abacus as a pillow; they hook and snatch at every fraction of a penny.

Yet their entire mental effort is devoted solely to the affairs of gold and grain. Such a crew—neither right nor wrong—rushes up and down, yet alas, they remain utterly unaware of what lies beneath their feet.
The Lord Feng of Baonan said: "A silk robe spun from raw silk and a fur-lined coat—how truly fine they look when one is dressed up.
Yet, when suddenly questioned about the Barrier of the Patriarchs, one is like Old Mistress Wang of the Eastern Village. This verse serves as the conclusion for today’s discourse.
Will this great event of today actually be carried out? Even if it were carried out, it would be in vain. It is like mending the penfold after the sheep have been lost.
"What can possibly remedy this? What can possibly remedy this? I replied: "What you have so fully set forth is not something I dare to deliberate upon.
In these late autumn days of the monastic groves, the five petals fall to the ground; the eight winds cut the skin to the bone, and demonic poison festers within the breast.
In every monastery one reaches, the dead are beyond counting. Nevertheless, amidst thousands and tens of thousands, if but one divine physician could be found..."
Using this to produce a single grain of elixir of immortality (*huandan*), who would suffer from its failure to restore life or bring back the soul?
You should know that this is specifically a formula for reviving the dead and a remedy for prolonging life. A divine physician may lack a miraculous pill, yet he cannot dispense with these [methods];
the meaning lies therein as well.
Written by Xingsheng Xin at Meling on the eve of the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of Xinwei, the Eiroku era, in the Linxuan Pavilion of Maga Forest.
